Over the next four decades, the figures for the USA and Sweden increased steadily to around 15% and 14% respectively by 1980. By contrast, Japan’s proportion fell to about 3% in the 1960s and then stayed almost unchanged until around 1990.

From 1980 onwards, the American figure edged down slightly and then remained stable at about 14% until 2020, before climbing to approximately 23% in 2040. Sweden followed a more fluctuating path, dipping a little in the 1990s, then rising to around 20% by 2010, falling modestly thereafter, and finally reaching about 25% at the end of the period. The diagrams illustrate the life cycle of the silkworm and the process used to produce silk cloth.

Overall, the silkworm passes through four main stages, from egg to moth, in a cyclical process lasting several weeks, while silk cloth is made by processing the cocoon through a series of mechanical stages. Notably, the cocoon is the key link between the natural cycle and the manufacturing process.

In the first diagram, adult moths lay eggs, which take around 10 days to hatch into silkworm larvae. These larvae feed on mulberry leaves and grow for 4 to 6 weeks. They then begin producing silk thread and, over the next 3 to 8 days, form a cocoon around themselves. After a further 16 days, an adult moth emerges from the cocoon, and the cycle starts again.

The second diagram shows that silk cloth production begins with the selection of suitable cocoons. These are boiled in water, after which the silk filaments are unwound. Each cocoon can yield a thread measuring approximately 300 to 900 metres. The thread is then twisted and woven into fabric. Dyeing can take place either at the thread stage or after the silk has been woven into cloth.

The diagrams illustrate the stages involved in producing cement and the way this material is then used to make concrete for construction.

Overall, cement manufacture is a linear, multi-stage process that requires several pieces of equipment and the application of heat, whereas concrete is produced in a single step by mixing four materials in fixed proportions.

To begin with, limestone and clay are fed into a crusher, where they are reduced to powder. This powdered material then passes into a mixer, after which it enters a rotating heater. Heat is applied at one end of this device while the drum turns, allowing the mixture to be processed thoroughly. The resulting material is subsequently transferred to a grinder, which produces the finished cement. Finally, the cement is packed into bags.

Concrete production is considerably simpler. Four ingredients are poured into a concrete mixer: gravel, which accounts for half of the mixture, sand at 25%, cement at 15%, and water at the remaining 10%. As the mixer rotates, these components are combined to form concrete. Thus, while cement is one of the raw materials used in concrete, it must first undergo a much more complex manufacturing process.

The diagrams illustrate the life cycle of salmon, showing the habitats they occupy, the time spent in each location, and their growth in size.

Overall, salmon pass through three main stages, beginning as eggs in the upper river and ending as fully grown adults that return there to reproduce. During this cycle, they migrate from freshwater to the open sea and increase markedly in length.

At the first stage, salmon eggs are laid among reeds and small stones in the slow-moving upper river. After approximately five to six months, the eggs hatch and the young fish, known as fry, emerge. These measure about 3 to 8 cm and move downstream to the fast-flowing lower river.

The fry remain in the lower river for around four years, during which they grow into smolt. By this stage, their size has risen to roughly 12 to 15 cm. The smolt then migrate to the open sea, where they spend a further five years developing into adult salmon.

In the final stage, adult salmon, which are considerably larger at about 70 to 76 cm in length, swim back upstream to the upper river. There, they lay eggs in the same kind of sheltered environment, and the cycle begins again.

The diagram illustrates how electricity is generated in a geothermal power plant.

Overall, the process consists of five main stages, beginning with the injection of cold water deep underground and ending with the production of electricity. In essence, water is heated by hot rocks below the surface, converted into steam, and then used to drive machinery above ground.

First, cold water stored at the surface is pumped down around 4.5 kilometres through the injection well. After reaching the geothermal zone, a layer of hot rocks, the water passes horizontally through this underground area and absorbs heat. It is then forced back up to the surface via a second shaft known as the production well.

Next, the hot water enters a condenser, where it is transformed into steam. This steam is directed into a turbine, causing the blades to spin. The turbine is connected to a generator, and as the turbine rotates, it powers the generator to produce electricity.

Finally, the electricity generated is transmitted from the power plant to the grid for distribution. Thus, the system relies on subterranean heat energy to create a continuous sequence from water circulation to electricity generation.

The diagram illustrates the process by which a hydroelectric power station generates electricity, showing different operations during the day and at night.

Overall, the system is based on the movement of water between two reservoirs at different heights. In daytime, water flows downhill from the upper reservoir to produce electricity, whereas at night the process is reversed and the water is pumped back uphill for reuse.

During the day, river water is stored behind a dam in a high-level reservoir. At this stage, the intake gate is opened, allowing water to pass down a conduit towards the power station. As the water moves downward, it drives reversible turbines, which in turn operate a generator located inside the station. The electricity produced is then transmitted by power lines to the national grid. After passing through the turbines, the water is discharged into a low-level reservoir.

At night, when electricity is not being generated, the intake at the dam is closed. The same reversible turbines then function as pumps, forcing water in the opposite direction from the lower reservoir back to the high-level reservoir. This creates a continuous cycle, enabling the station to store water and generate power again the following day.

The diagram illustrates the process used to manufacture instant noodles.

Overall, it is a linear, eight-stage procedure that begins with storing flour and ends with sealing and labelling the finished cups. Broadly, the first half of the process involves preparing and shaping the dough, while the later stages focus on cooking the noodles and packaging them with flavourings.

Initially, flour is kept in large storage silos before being transferred to a mixer. At this point, water and oil are added, and the resulting dough is then passed through a series of rollers. These flatten it into dough sheets, which are subsequently cut into narrow strips. The strips are then formed into individual noodle discs.

Next, these discs are cooked in oil and dried. Once this has been done, the dried noodle portions are placed into cups. Vegetables and spices are added to each cup at the packaging stage, after which the containers are labelled and sealed. The final output is a set of ready-to-sell cups of instant noodles.

In short, raw flour is gradually transformed into packaged noodles through a sequence of mixing, rolling, cutting, cooking and packing stages.

Notably, the crop can be harvested in two different ways, after which the extracted juice is purified, concentrated and separated before sugar is obtained.

First, sugar cane is cultivated for between one year and a year and a half until it is ready for harvest. At this stage, farmers either cut the stalks by hand or use a machine to collect them. The harvested cane is then fed into a crusher, where the juice is squeezed out.

Next, this raw liquid passes through a limestone filter in order to remove impurities. Once purified, the juice is heated in an evaporator, which causes water to evaporate and turns the liquid into a thicker syrup. The syrup is subsequently placed in a centrifuge, whose spinning action separates sugar crystals from the remaining syrup.

In the final stage, these crystals are dried and cooled in a large container, producing the finished sugar ready for use.
